title: Quantum simulacra
authors: L. F. Alves da Silva, M. H. Y. Moussa
abstract: Here we analyze the creation of quantum simulacra: phenomena that emerge from treating a Hermitian or non-Hermitian quantum system in metrics other than the standard $L^{2}$. Changing the metric redefines the set of system observables and thus the experimental arrangement for their measurement, making quantum contextuality and microscopic reality metric-dependent. The simulacra therefore consist, on the one hand, of a resizing of the status of quantum measurement, which has always occupied a central role in quantum mechanics: beyond the connection between quantum and classical dynamics, measurements performed in an appropriate metric can emulate a microscopic reality distinct from that prescribed by the Hamiltonian. On the other hand, simulacra provide a route to implementing quantum operations that lie beyond the reach of the $L^2$ metric. Quantum simulacra offer, as an example, an explanation for the recent observation of the violation of Bell inequalities with unentangled photons [Sci. Adv. \textbf{11}, eadr1794 (2025)]: photons that are separable in $L^2$ metric, become entangled when analyzed within a new metric framework. Simulacrum comes at the cost of implementing measurements of the metric-redefined observables; to address this challenge, we propose a scheme combining positive operator-valued measures with postselected subensembles.
summary: The paper introduces 'quantum simulacra,' demonstrating how changing the mathematical metric used to measure a quantum system can make it appear to exhibit properties—like entanglement or superradiance—that are not present in its underlying Hamiltonian. This is achieved by combining advanced measurement techniques (POVMs with postselection) with a metric operator $\Theta$, suggesting that experimental context fundamentally shapes perceived physical reality.
main_problem: The paper analyzes 'quantum simulacra': phenomena that emerge when quantum systems are analyzed using metrics other than the standard L2 norm.
main_result: By redefining the measurement metric ($\Theta$), one can generate observable effects, such as Bell violations with unentangled photons or superradiant phase transitions, that are absent in the standard Hamiltonian description.
method: The analysis adapts pseudo-Hermitian quantum mechanics frameworks, utilizing a positive-definite metric operator $\Theta$ and combining Positive Operator-Valued Measures (POVM) with postselected subensembles for measurement.
model_or_system: The work applies to various systems, including radiation-field modes (squeezing), two-level systems (entanglement/Bell tests), and the Tavis–Cummings model. The core concept involves modifying the inner product via $\Theta$.
key_observables: Correlation functions $E(\varphi_A, \varphi_B)$, Concurrence ($C$), squeezing quadratures ($\Delta X_\ell$), and photon number ($\hat{n}$).
important_parameters: The metric choice is parametrized by $\zeta$ (or related parameters in the Tavis-Cummings model), which dictates whether a simulacrum manifests.
main_assumptions: The procedure critically relies on combining POVMs with postselection to enforce the use of the non-standard metric $\Theta$ during measurement, rather than assuming it is inherent to the Hamiltonian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 'POVM + postselection' scheme for continuous quadratures and show theoretical uncertainties ($\Delta X_\ell$) versus a parameter $\zeta$.
paper_structure: The paper builds from general principles of metric-dependent observables, applies this to specific examples like squeezing and entanglement (showing simulacra), and culminates in demonstrating the feasibility of superradiant phase transitions via metric engineering.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful conceptual tool showing that physical reality is not solely determined by the Hamiltonian but can be engineered or revealed through the choice of measurement framework (the metric).
